title: Pipeline for fluorescent imaging and volumetric analysis of neurons in cleared mouse spinal cords
protocol: Mix 1 mL of ketamine (100 mg/mL), 0.1 mL of xylazine (100 mg/mL) and bring to 10 mL with normal 0.9% saline to create anesthetic solution.
Ensure the final solution contains 10 mg/mL of ketamine and 1 mg/mL of xylazine.
Dissolve 500 μg of solid CTB tracer in 100 μL of 1x PBS, pH 7.2.
Gently mix the CTB tracer solution until fully dissolved.
Spin the solution in a centrifuge for 2 seconds at 1000 x g.
Keep the CTB tracer solution on ice until ready to use.
Aliquot the CTB tracer solution into 2.5 μL aliquots and store at -20°C for up to 3 months.
Prepare surgical equipment and operating area according to institutional guidelines.
Pull glass capillaries (1.0 mm Outer Diameter) into needles with a micropipette puller (Program 14).
Trim excess length from pulled needle tips for muscle injections, aiming for approximately 7 mm in length.
Smoothen the needle tips using a micropipette beveler.
Intraperitoneally inject anesthetic solution into the mouse using a 26G 3/8 needle (0.1 mL/10 g body weight).
Shave the mouse’s back from lower neck to hip until devoid of hair.
Remove any hair stubs using Nair.
Scrub the exposed skin several times with 10% povidone iodine.
Disinfect the region again with 70% ethanol.
Apply triple antibiotic ointment to the mouse’s eyes.
Secure the animal in the stereotaxic device.
Place a blunt ear bar into the mouse’s right ear canal and tighten.
Repeat the process by placing an ear bar into the left ear and tightening.
Secure the mouse’s upper incisors in the mouth holder.
Adjust the apparatus until the mouse head position is level.
Disinfect the surgical site using povidone iodine and ethanol again.
Drape sterile towels over the operating area.
Make a sagittal incision along the midline of the back where the external oblique muscle is located.
Retract the skin away from the midline to expose the muscle layer.
Secure the retracted skin with surgical hooks and identify the external oblique muscles.
Load CTB tracer solution into the tracer injection apparatus.
Connect a glass needle to the Hamilton syringe to create the injection apparatus.
Slowly load a minimum of 5 μL of tracer solution into the micropipette.
Ensure there are no air bubbles in the injection apparatus before proceeding.
Attach the injection apparatus to the syringe pump.
Inject CTB tracer into the external oblique muscle bilaterally.
Determine the amount of tracer solution to inject and set the automated syringe pump accordingly.
Identify and mark the first injection site on one side using a marker.
Slowly insert the needle into the muscle and inject 2 μL of tracer.
Remove the needle slowly from the muscle to prevent tracer solution backflow due to negative pressure.
Label the desired contralateral injection site using a marker.
Inject 2 μL of tracer into the labeled site.
Perform 3 additional injections of tracer solution at the initial injection site.
Repeat the process for the contralateral muscle.
Close surgical incisions using staples.
Apply antibiotics along the incision line.
Wait 3 days before perfusing for tissue clearing.
Post-fix spinal cords in 4% PFA after whole body perfusion.
Perform delipidation on the fixed spinal cord using CUBIC-L.
Match refractive index of the sample with CUBIC-R+(M).
Mount the cleared spinal cord sample in an agarose gel suitable for imaging.
Prepare a 1 mL syringe as a mold by removing its tip.
Pipette 2% CUBIC-R+(M) agarose into the prepared syringe.
Embed a cleared sample in the agarose within the syringe.
Allow the gel to polymerize completely.
Lower the embedded sample for imaging after gel solidification.
Prepare D-PBS and 4% PFA solution for whole body perfusion.
To make 2 liters of 4% PFA, add 160 g of PFA to 2 L ultrapure H2O in a 4 L Erlenmeyer flask.
Stir the mixture until the PFA is fully dissolved at 60°C.
Allow the solution to cool to room temperature before use.
Prepare anesthetic solution by mixing ketamine, xylazine, and normal saline (1 mL:0.1 mL:8.5 mL).
Inject the anesthetic solution intraperitoneally into the mouse using a 26G 3/8 needle (0.1 mL/10 g body weight).
Wait for the mouse to become fully anesthetized before proceeding.
Pre-chill D-PBS and 4% PFA solutions in an ice bath prior to use.
Fill perfusion system tubing with cold D-PBS before starting the procedure.
Secure the mouse.
Open the chest cavity to expose the heart.
Insert the perfusion needle into the left ventricle carefully.
Perfuse with cold D-PBS at 18 mL/min for 30 seconds, total of 9 mL.
Continue perfusing with cold D-PBS at 10 mL/min for 60 seconds, total of 10 mL.
Perfuse with cold PFA at 10 mL/min for 2 minutes, total of 20 mL.
Dissect the spinal cord immediately after successful perfusion and place it in 10 mL of cold 4% PFA.
Shake the conical tube containing the spinal cords at 150 RPM at 4°C for 12–24 hours post-fixation.
Minimize exposure of spinal cords to light during fixation.
Remove the spinal cord from the PFA.
Dissect the spinal cord dura carefully without damaging the spinal cord.
Rinse the sample with 1x PBS to remove debris.
Isolate the segment of interest for cervical or lumbar regions by dissecting the spinal region with the corresponding enlargement.
If interested in the thoracic region, isolate the spinal segment between the cervical and lumbar enlargements.
Transfer the spinal cord segments into a 2 mL cryotube vial.
Wash the samples to remove PFA using PBS with 0.01% (wt/vol) sodium azide by shaking at 150 RPM on an orbital shaker at room temperature for 2 h.
Replace with fresh PBS and continue washing for an additional 2 h.
Replace again with fresh PBS and continue washing for a final 2 h.
Ensure the samples are not stuck to the cap or sides of the vial during washing steps.
Store fixed spinal cords at -80°C.
Place the spinal cords in a 15 mL conical tube with 10 mL of 30% (wt/vol) sucrose.
Gently shake the tube at 4°C until spinal cords sink to the bottom, which may take up to 24 hours.
Embed spinal cords in OCT compound and store at -80°C for up to 6 months.
Thaw samples at room temperature (20°C).
Repeat PBS wash to remove OCT (step 14c) after thawing.
Prepare half-diluted CUBIC-L solution by mixing equal volumes of CUBIC-L with ultrapure H2O.
Stir the mixture for 5 minutes in a jar containing a small stir bar.
Immerse each spinal cord segment in 2 mL of half-diluted CUBIC-L and shake at 150 RPM at 37°C for 12–24 hours.
Replace with fresh 1x CUBIC-L, shaking at 150 RPM at 37°C for 24 hours.
Replace with fresh 1x CUBIC-L again and shake at 150 RPM at 37°C for an additional 24 hours.
Replace with 2 mL of fresh 1x CUBIC-L and shake at 150 RPM at 37°C for a final 24 h.
Wash the samples to remove residual CUBIC-L.
Replace CUBIC-L with 2 mL of PBS with 0.01% (wt/vol) sodium azide and shake at 150 RPM at room temperature (20°C) for 2 h.
Replace with 2 mL of fresh PBS and continue washing for an additional 2 h.
Prepare half-diluted CUBIC-R+(M): Mix equal volumes of CUBIC-R+(M) with ultrapure H2O.
Make 2 mL of half-diluted CUBIC-R+(M) for each 4 mm spinal cord segment.
Add a small stir bar to a 50 mL jar.
Add 10 mL ultrapure H2O and 10 mL CUBIC-R+(M) to the jar.
Stir the mixture for 5 minutes.
Immerse samples in 2 mL of half-diluted CUBIC-R+(M).
Shake at 150 RPM at room temperature (20°C) for 12–24 hours.
Replace with 2 mL of fresh CUBIC-R+(M).
Shake at 150 RPM at room temperature (20°C) for 24 hours.
Replace with another 2 mL of fresh CUBIC-R+(M).
Shake at 150 RPM at room temperature (20°C) for a final 24 hours.
Thoroughly dissolve 2% (wt/wt) agarose powder in CUBIC-R+(M) at room temperature by vigorous stirring.
Add 0.11 g of agarose to 5.4 ml of CUBIC-R+(M) solution in a lidded glass jar to make 5 ml of gel.
Heat the mixture using a microwave until it just starts to boil, then remove and cover immediately.
Stir vigorously until the agarose dissolves and the gel becomes transparent.
Pipette 400 μl of agarose-CUBIC-R+(M) solution into a 1 ml syringe to make a 20 mm (0.3 ml) long base.
Cover the syringe with parafilm and leave at room temperature for 1 hour.
Transfer 100–200 μL of agarose-CUBIC-R+(M) solution into a 1 mL syringe to make a top layer gel.
Gently pipette out any bubbles from the agarose-CUBIC-R+(M) solution.
Remove the sample from its vial using a soft brush.
Using the brush, gently guide the sample towards the center of the syringe and slide it into the gel top layer.
Manipulate the sample with the brush until it is in the desired orientation.
Cover the syringe with parafilm and leave in the dark at room temperature for 1 hour.
Keep the gel-embedded sample in the dark to prevent fluorophore bleaching.
Make a new batch of gel for each run to ensure imaging quality.
Image cleared spinal cords using the Zeiss Z7 LSFM.
Separate the specimen into tiles with 10% overlap for volumetric imaging.
Optimize tile size to balance accuracy, resolution, and efficiency.
Initialize the microscope.
Power on the microscope and acquisition system.
Start Zen Black 3.1 software with the appropriate hardware database (.mdb).

Check the “Maintain” tab to ensure correct detection and illumination lenses are selected (5X, 0.16 NA variable refractive index detection objective and 5X, 0.1 NA variable refractive index illumination objective).
Open the chamber door.
Install the 5X, 0.16 NA variable refractive index imaging lens into the microscope with the refractive index set to n=1.52.
Ensure there is no sample in the imaging chamber during initialization to avoid damage.
Install the 5X, 0.1 NA variable refractive index illumination lenses with the same refractive index as the imaging lens (n=1.52).
Install the imaging chamber on the dovetail track and secure it with the set screw.
Fill a 50 mL Luer Lok syringe with fresh CUBIC-R+(M) solution.
Connect the syringe to the microscope imaging chamber using tubing.
Fill the imaging chamber to cover the imaging coverglass windows with CUBIC-R+(M).
Close the chamber door, taking care not to overfill and cause spills.
Locate the tissue sample and orient it in front of the microscope’s imaging lens.
Set the microscope stage to “Load” position.
Open the microscope’s top door.
Insert a 1 mL syringe into the appropriate sample holder.
Couple the syringe to the microscope stage using magnetic clips with white lines aligned on both the sample holder and stage.
Close the top door of the microscope.
Navigate to the “Locate” tab and start “Overview”.
Use the specimen navigator to control the stage.
Lower the syringe until just a small tip is visible in the overview panel.
Leave some travel on the y-axis rather than lowering the syringe completely.
Open the top door.
Gently push the syringe’s plunger down until the sample region is centered in the overview panel.
Close the top door.
Press the “Overview” button once more to shut down the webcam.
Mark start and end positions on the plunger before mounting it in the microscope.
Press “Locate Sample” to illuminate the sample with near-infrared LEDs.
Capture transmitted light images with the imaging objective.
Zoom out to increase field of view.
Move the sample near the illustrated focus of the imaging objective marked with a blue sheet.
Adjust the light intensity and display settings for good contrast until you see a focused image of the spinal cord.
Orient the sample using the specimen navigator until the desired orientation for fluorescence imaging is reached.
Typically orient the ventral spinal cord toward the imaging objective to minimize tissue between the objective and planes of interest.
Flatten the imaging volume to minimize the number of slices and acquisition time.
Rotate to a different angle if bubbles or defects in agarose obscure labeled neurons.
Turn off "Locate Sample".
Initialize the lasers and set up the acquisition parameters.
Turn on the lasers with the best excitation lines.
Use the 561 nm laser to visualize ChAT-Ai14 samples (tdTomato labeled motor neurons).
Use the 631 nm laser to visualize CTB-647 samples (retrogradely labeled motor neurons).
Enumerate the correct “Light Path”.
Select the appropriate emission filter cube, such as the “LP 640/BP 575-615/LP 660”.
Check the camera (channel 1 or channel 2) that you will be imaging with.
Set acquisition mode parameters: Bit depth to 16 bit.
Light sheet to “Dual side when experiment”.
Direction to either “Left” or “Right”.
Select “online dual side fusion” and pick the “mean” fusion method.
Ensure “Pivot Scan” is selected.
Frame size to 1920 × 1920.
Set the desired colormap for each channel.
Ensure the correct excitation laser(s) is/are checked on for the correct track(s).
Set the laser power to a low value initially, between 5-10% laser power.
Note and adjust the camera exposure time as needed after light sheet alignment.
Align the light sheets.
Optimize light sheet offset values for individual tracks to reduce chromatic aberration if necessary.
Position the sample with low laser power to avoid bleaching.
Increase brightness and contrast under the display panel if image is difficult to see.
Select the appropriate track corresponding to the laser used.
Align each track to the same focal plane in z sequentially.
For tdTomato labeled samples, select the track for the 561 nm laser and set the display color to red.
For CTB-647 samples, select the track for the 638 nm laser and set the display color to gray.
Turn on “Continuous” mode.
Adjust the laser intensity and camera exposure time until the sample is clearly visible with low laser power but the exposure is not too long.
Navigate to a superficial position within the sample using single-side illumination (left or right).
Click in the box where the light-sheet offset is located and use the up and down arrow keys to move the light sheet through the sample, adjusting the sample position if it runs out of range.
Continue moving the light sheet until the image begins to defocus again.
Switch directions and bring the light sheet back to the middle of the focus once one side is in focus.
Choose a group of cells to serve as reference markers for bringing the other side into the same focal plane.
Digitally zoom in if needed at this step.
Switch to the other side illumination.
Adjust the light sheet offset to match the image to the reference image from step e.
Move to other locations within the sample and switch between left/right illumination to check co-alignment quality.
Collect a small z-stack using dual-side illumination and online dual-side fusion.
Examine the quality of the resulting image volume.
Try different fusion options, aiming for the best result (for example, "mean").
If structures are doubled or too elongated along the z-axis, adjust the sheets to bring them closer to the same plane.
Collect a sample z-stack again until the result is optimized.
Switch tracks and enter the offsets found for the track used for alignment.
Collect a dual-track dataset to check that all illumination sides, color channels, and tracks are imaging the same plane.
If the tracks are misaligned, perform alignment as described in b-i above for the second track, aiming for the same focal plane.
Collect another test dataset and repeat until both tracks image the same plane.
Set up the vertical z-stacks by checking the “Z-stack” box under the acquisition tab to enable vertical tiling.
Under the Z-stack panel, select “First/Last”.
Move the overview to the top left corner of the sample.
Set the zoom to 0.36 X.
Move the sample away from the detection objective until the end of the sample is reached.
Set this position as “last”.
Move the sample through the focus of the detection objective in the opposite direction until the end is reached.
Set this position as “first”.
Shift the field of view and check if the previously determined first and last points need to be adjusted to ensure there is no clipping.
Zoom to 1.6X, or whichever zoom planned for individual tiles.
Click the “Optimal” button to set the optimal slice thickness.
Under the acquisition tab, check the “Tiling” box to enable horizontal and vertical tiling.
Select “Bounding grid” method to enumerate the tiles.
Set “Overlap” to 10%.
Move the sample to the top left corner and press “add” to record this position as the first point of the bounding box.
Move the camera to the bottom right corner and “add” it as the second point of the bounding box.
Scroll horizontally and vertically from the top left or bottom right edge of the sample to ensure all of the sample is enclosed.
Click on “Start Experiment” to create a file name and begin image acquisition.
Use the Imaris surfaces tool powered by a machine learning algorithm to quantify the number and volume of fluorescently labeled neurons.
Train Labkit AI to recognize different cells and exclude background when determining cell boundaries.
Measure diameters of labeled cells in slice mode by drawing a line from the midpoint of one edge through the center to the opposite end.
Mark pixels that make up the cell soma as foreground using the red foreground label with a brush size of 1.
Label background pixels and those that make up the axons using the blue background label with a brush size of 1.
Convert raw image file from .czi to multi-resolution, chunked .ims format.
Add raw image files into Imaris File Converter.
Press “Start All” to convert the files.
Ensure each raw image’s output folder is unique to prevent file mix-ups.
Unstitch the individual converted tiles into multiple .ims image pyramid files.
Add the .ims tiles into Imaris Stitcher.
Check the positioning of the tiles on the screen.
Manually drag the tiles until satisfied with their placement if there are any issues with overlap.
Align and stitch the images with “Align All Images”.
Check the aligned image for alignment problems and realign if necessary.
Save the stitched image when you are satisfied with the alignment.
Determine an estimated cell diameter for the population of labeled cells.
Switch Imaris to “Slice” view.
Measure the cell diameter of 30 randomly selected cells according to the following steps.
Adjust the slice viewed until the thickest region of the selected cell is in view.
Start the measurement at the midpoint of one edge of the cell, and end at the opposite side.
Make sure the line crosses the center of the cell.
Repeat this for 30 randomly selected cells.
Average all their diameters to obtain the estimated average value.
Create a new surface object in Imaris.
Isolate the cells of interest.
Use the “Segment only a Region of Interest” feature in “3D View” to isolate the volume containing the cells of interest.
Scroll through the image slices and look for cells.
Using the foreground brush with brush size set to 1, draw a line from one end of the cell to the other, crossing the center point of the cell.
Mark at least two other cells on the same slice using the foreground brush, ensuring they have different intensity levels.
Mark the image background in Labkit using sparse manual labels on the same z-stack as the foreground.
Label axons as background.
Label artifacts as background.
Label the image background itself as background.
Distinguish axons from cells.
Using the background brush with brush size set to 1, trace the axons of at least 3 cells to mark them as background.
For each cell labeled as “foreground”, draw a short line close to but not touching the soma using the background brush.
Find three areas of the image that are obviously background.
Draw a short line using the background brush in each of these areas.
Repeat sparse labeling steps on two additional slices to help refine training.
Scroll through the image and find another slice where there are many cells in focus.
Using sparse manual labeling, repeat the foreground and background labeling steps.
Maintain consistency when labeling different slices.
Click on the “Labkit Pixel Classification” button under segmentation.
Reveal additional options by clicking on the “Labkit Pixel Classification” button.
Begin training the algorithm based on marked foreground and background by clicking the “Play” button.
Once the algorithm finishes training, turn on or off the red/blue overlay by clicking the eye icon for the segmentation panel.
Scroll through the slices and note what the algorithm has denoted as foreground and background.
Use either of the tools to correct misidentifications.
Pay attention to how well the cell boundaries are defined and if axons have been marked as foreground.
When dealing with cell somas of varying intensities, use either the foreground or background brushes to make amendments.
Train the machine learning algorithm again with the corrections.
Take note of the result after retraining.
Repeat the correction and training steps until satisfied with the results of the algorithm.
Click “Compute results and send it to Imaris” to send the foreground and background information to Imaris for surface creation.
Set the default filter on the filter panel to "Quality".
Add a volume filter with a lower threshold of 10,000 μm3.
Finish surface creation by executing all creation steps and terminating the wizard.
Unify split cell surfaces using the single selection tool under the “Navigation” pane.
Select all parts of the split cell in the edit tab and click on "Unify".
Export volumetric data to an Excel file from the “Detailed” statistics main tab.
In the drop-down menu, select “Specific Values”, then choose “Volume”.
Use the “Export Statistics on Tab Display to File” function for exporting data.
Export numeric data to an Excel file under the “Overall” statistics main tab.
Export statistics on tab display to file to obtain volumetric data in an Excel file.
Calculate cell density using the total cell count.
Switch Imaris to slice view and measure the entire quantified length of the sample.
Divide the total number of cells by the respective length to determine the cell density.
